title: Sanjeev Kapoor's Honey Chilli Baby Corn Brings the Indo-Chinese Classic Home
excerpt: The celebrity chef's sweet-and-spicy starter uses a double-coating technique for extra crunch and a quick Oriental sauce that comes together in under 40 minutes.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Sanjeev Kapoor's recipe features a two-step coating for extra crunch in honey chilli baby corn.
  • The dish takes about 35 minutes to prepare and serves four without special equipment.
  • Honey is added off the heat to maintain its sweetness and prevent bitterness.
  • The recipe has gained popularity on Sanjeev Kapoor's Khazana platform and food communities.

  • Chef Sanjeev Kapoor's honey chilli baby corn recipe uses a two-step coating — a dry spice mix followed by a refined flour batter — for maximum crunch that holds up under the sauce.
  • The Indo-Chinese dish takes about 35 minutes from start to plate, serves four, and requires no specialized equipment beyond a kadai and a pan.
  • The key technique is adding honey off the heat at the end, which preserves its floral sweetness and prevents it from turning bitter or caramelizing too quickly.
  • The recipe originally appeared on Sanjeev Kapoor's Khazana platform and has been widely shared across Indian food communities online.

Few dishes sit as comfortably at the intersection of Indian and Chinese cooking as honey chilli baby corn. The snack is a staple of Indo-Chinese restaurant menus across India and in diaspora kitchens worldwide — crispy, glazed, and built around a balance of sweet heat that makes it vanish from the plate within minutes. Chef Sanjeev Kapoor's version, shared on his Khazana platform, strips the dish down to a home-friendly method without losing the restaurant-quality crunch.

The Double-Coating Technique

What separates a good honey chilli baby corn from a soggy one is the coating. Kapoor's method starts by halving 10 to 12 baby corns vertically and rolling them in a dry mixture of corn flour, rice flour, onion powder, garlic powder, salt, and crushed black peppercorns. This first layer draws out surface moisture and creates a gritty base for the batter to grip.

https://x.com/htlifeandstyle/status/2079595075672412320

"Each coated baby corn gets dipped in this batter and slid into hot oil in a kadai, where it fries to a golden, audibly crisp finish."

The second layer is a simple batter of refined flour (maida), salt, and crushed peppercorns whisked with water until smooth. Each coated baby corn gets dipped in this batter and slid into hot oil in a kadai, where it fries to a golden, audibly crisp finish. The dual coating is what gives the pieces their staying power — they remain crunchy even after being tossed in a wet sauce.

Building the Sauce

The sauce comes together quickly in a separate pan. A tablespoon and a half of oil goes in first, followed by finely chopped garlic and ginger sautéed for a minute or two. Chopped red and green chillies and spring onion bulbs go in next, cooking until fragrant. Red chilli paste is stirred in with a quarter cup of water, then red chilli sauce, soy sauce, and vinegar are added in quick succession.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=_zD9Ifez8Zk

Sliced spring onion greens and the fried baby corns are tossed into this mixture until everything is coated. The heat is then switched off — and this is the step that matters most. The honey goes in only after the flame is killed, along with toasted white sesame seeds. Adding honey off the heat preserves its floral notes and prevents the sugars from burning or turning acrid.

The Perfect Coating Technique
›First layer: Dry spice mix with corn flour and rice flour.
›Second layer: Refined flour batter for extra crunch.
›Dual coating keeps baby corn crispy after saucing.
›Honey added off heat preserves sweetness.

Serving and Variations

The dish is garnished with more spring onion greens and a final scatter of sesame seeds before serving hot. Total time from prep to plate is about 35 minutes, and it serves four as a starter.

https://www.instagram.com/p/DazesHWCN5c/

Indo-Chinese cooking — a cuisine born in Kolkata's Chinatown in the mid-20th century and now found in restaurants from Mumbai to New Jersey — thrives on this kind of dish: a handful of accessible ingredients, a fast technique, and a flavor profile that hits sweet, salty, sour, and spicy in every bite. Kapoor's version keeps it simple enough for a weeknight but polished enough for a monsoon dinner party.

"Baby corns absorb the flavours of the ingredients they are cooked with. This is a delicious recipe where they are batter fried till crisp and then tossed in a flavourful Oriental sauce and finished with a generous drizzle of honey."

— Sanjeev Kapoor, sanjeevkapoor.com

The recipe works equally well with cauliflower florets, paneer cubes, or mushrooms substituted for baby corn, following the same coating and sauce method. For a lighter version, some home cooks have adapted it for the air fryer — though Kapoor's original calls for the deep-fried crunch that defines the Indo-Chinese original.
